newsitem.title: USA: Muni bar at "pay-to-play" ethics crossroads - Levitt.
newsitem.headline: Muni bar at "pay-to-play" ethics crossroads - Levitt.

text.p: Citing growing public cynicism towards lawyers, SEC's chairman on Thursday urged attorneys nationwide to adopt a New York City bar proposal to end "pay-to-play" by municipal bond lawyers.

"Shady practices in the municipal market today have placed lawyers at an ethical crossroads," Arthur Levitt told market participants meeting in Philadelphia, according to a written text of the Securities and Exchange Commission chief's address.
"A simple question is crystallizing: Will lawyers act to end 'pay-to-play,' or will they rationalize, temporize, and dodge the issue?" Levitt said in his written speech.

Levitt wants American Bar Association delegates meeting in San Francisco in August to adopt a tough ban on pay-to-play proposed earlier this year by the Association of the Bar of the City of New York.
Pay-to-play refers to municipal bond professionals who make contributions to elected municipal officials in return for a crack at bond business.
Levitt offered a "real-life example" of pay-to-play told to him by former SEC General Counsel Simon Lorne.

"An investment banker told me that a state political figure (said) they needed to make a five-figure contribution to his campaign, or be excluded from all state finance activities," Lorne said, according to Levitt.

"They asked me what they should do," Lorne continued. "I was shocked by the question. After considerable research ... I was forced to tell them that the answer was probably to write a check. There was no clear illegality. I did not like giving that answer," Lorne said, according to Levitt.

Levitt said that a National Association of Bond Lawyers resolution reminding attorneys not to make contributions in return for bond business has "no teeth." The National Law Journal called it "a joke," Levitt added.
"Some have said, 'It's not my problem - tell the issuers to stop asking for money.' But true character lies in accepting responsibility, not shunning it," Levitt said.

As for those lawyers who want more evidence of pay-to-play before they act, Levitt said, "Can the lawyers really be blind to what the dealers see?" he said. He was referring to a voluntary pay-to-play ban adopted by dealers four years ago.

Levitt said the City bar's proposal is fairly simple. "None of this is rocket science. The resolution would ask bond lawyers to cut the tie between campaign contributions and selection as bond counsel."
"Yet, several lawyers have voiced strong opposition," Levitt said.

Larry Fox, head of ABA's influential standing committee on ethics, is one of several key association officials who strongly object to the City bar's plan for various reasons, including warnings that it may be unconstitutional.
But Levitt noted that courts have upheld the constitutionality of similar measures developed for bond dealers.

"There are good lawyers on both sides of this question," Levitt continued. "But even good lawyers can sometimes become so mired in the details of a proposal that they lose sight of the goal," Levitt said.
"This is not a time for good lawyers. This is a time for great lawyers. I hope they will heed our call," Levitt said.
